subject: Positive definiteness failure on initialization causes crash rather than rejection

messages.author: 37450357c92565e5
messages.subject: Positive definiteness failure on initialization causes crash rather than rejection
parts:
I'm fitting a model that parameterizes a covariance matrix.  The model works fine and converges to the true parameter values (from simulated data)...as long as it makes it past initialization.  If the initial values make the covariance matrix not positive definite, then it crashes with an error like this:

Error : Invalid value of Sigma: Error in function validate transformed params d: Sigma[k0__] is not positive definite. Sigma[k0__](0,0) is 1.3203452576620608e-08.
error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done


Is this expected behavior?  I would expect that it would simply reject the sample rather than crashing the sampler.  The same thing seems to happen occasionally during adaptation, and it does what I expect--it rejects the sample and issues this warning:

Informational Message: The parameter state is about to be Metropolis rejected due to the following underlying, non-fatal (really) issue (and please ignore that what comes next might say 'error'): Invalid value of Sigma: Error in function validate transformed params N4stan5agrad3varE: Sigma[k0__] is not symmetric. Sigma[k0__][0,1] is -4.9916394362858062e+134:0, but Sigma[k0__][1,0] element is -4.99164e+134:0
If the problem persists across multiple draws, you might have a problem with an initial state or a gradient somewhere.
 If the problem does not persist, the resulting samples will still be drawn from the posterior.


A little searching suggests that this was a known issue that was fixed a while back:
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/18
I'm on Stan 1.3, and the fix appears in the 1.3 milestone code, so maybe the fix didn't quite get everything?

In the spirit of that issue, the minimal model still causes a crash--it's the same situation I'm facing, and the minimal model is much simpler to reproduce:


parameters {
  corr_matrix[100] Omega;
}

transformed parameters {
  corr_matrix[100] Omega3;
  Omega3 <- Omega;
}

model {
}


This fails for me with the following error:

COMPILING THE C++ CODE FOR MODEL 'test_model' NOW.
SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'test_model' NOW (CHAIN 1).
Error : Invalid value of Omega3: Error in function validate transformed params d: y is not positive definite. y(0,0) is 1.
error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done


Not surprisingly, the same thing happens if I define Omega and Omega3 as cov_matrix rather than corr_matrix.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Positive definiteness failure on initialization causes crash rather than rejection
parts:
On 9/25/13 3:44 PM, Jon Smith wrote:

Is that John (like the e-mail) or Jon (like the name)
or is this a pseudonym and it doesn't matter?

> I'm fitting a model that parameterizes a covariance matrix. The model works fine and converges to the true parameter
> values (from simulated data)...as long as it makes it past initialization.
Are you providing initial values or letting them be assigned randomly?

> If the initial values make the covariance
> matrix not positive definite, then it crashes with an error like this:
>
> Error : Invalid value of Sigma: Error in function validate transformed params d: Sigma[k0__] is not positive
> definite. Sigma[k0__](0,0) is 1.3203452576620608e-08.
>
> error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done
>
>
> Is this expected behavior?

This isn't technically a crash (my bad in the original terminology).
It's an error that intentionally terminates the program with an error message.
We do it for error checking.

The underlying reason is that if you start outside of support,
there's no good way to move into support using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
because we can't calculate gradients.
> I would expect that it would simply reject the sample rather than crashing the sampler.

That would be nice, but we have no idea how to do that.

Perhaps for random init values for covariance matrices we could
add some regularlization to help with starting in a positive
definite matrix.

> The
> same thing seems to happen occasionally during adaptation, and it does what I expect--it rejects the sample and issues
> this warning:
>
> |
> Informational Message: The parameter state is about to be Metropolis rejected due to the following underlying,
> non-fatal (really) issue (and please ignore that what comes next might say 'error'): Invalid value of Sigma: Error
> in function validate transformed params N4stan5agrad3varE: Sigma[k0__] is not symmetric. Sigma[k0__][0,1] is
> -4.9916394362858062e+134:0, but Sigma[k0__][1,0] element is -4.99164e+134:0
> If the problem persists across multiple draws, you might have a problem with an initial state or a gradient somewhere.
> If the problem does not persist, the resulting samples will still be drawn from the posterior.
> |
>
>
> A little searching suggests that this was a known issue that was fixed a while back:
> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/18
> I'm on Stan 1.3, and the fix appears in the 1.3 milestone code, so maybe the fix didn't quite get everything?

Thanks for searching and letting us know which version you're using.
And for the detailed error report below.

The rejections after initialization are due to starting at a valid
in-support matrix, then moving along the gradient too far so you're
outside of support. That we can fix by rejecting and choosing another
direction at random.

> In the spirit of that issue, the minimal model still causes a crash--it's the same situation I'm facing, and the minimal
> model is much simpler to reproduce:
>
>
> |
> parameters {
> corr_matrix[100] Omega;
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
> corr_matrix[100] Omega3;
> Omega3 <- Omega;
> }
>
> model {
> }
> |

Thanks especially for the minimial code that replicates the problem.
Sometimes it's very tricky to do, but it's hugely helpful for us,
because it's the first thing we try to do when faced with huge user
models.

You shouldn't need the transformed parameters block here to
recreate the init errors.

>
> This fails for me with the following error:
>
> |
> COMPILING THE C++ CODE FOR MODEL 'test_model' NOW.
> SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'test_model' NOW (CHAIN 1).
> Error : Invalid value of Omega3: Error in function validate transformed params d: y is not positive definite. y(0,0) is 1.
> error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done

I take it that's with automatic inits? We definitely need
to make initialization for correlation matrices more robust.

One thing we can do is relax the stringency of the positive-definiteness
test. Floating-point is such a pain. With real values, we would
be guaranteed positive definiteness, but the rounding errors accumulate,
especially in high dimensions.

I'm creating an issue for it:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/240

We've frozen 2.0, so we probably won't fix it before the 2.0 beta,
but it's a high priority because we really want multivariate
models to work properly!

- Bob

Ah, that all makes sense--thanks!  

Yes, this only happens with random init values.  Adding some regularization or increasing the tolerance on the positive definiteness check would be great.  You could also draw new init values--I know Stan does this sometimes (I've run into the limit where it fails after 100 failed initialization attempts), though I can imagine it being helpful for this to continue to fail gracefully to help in diagnosing more serious modeling problems.

Thanks for the explanation and for creating the issue.  It's certainly not a showstopper--I can still get things to work fine by simply ignoring the chains with bad inits.  

I could also be less lazy and write my own initialization function--I've just avoided it because I'm still making a lot of changes to my own model.  On that note, I have a small RStan idea: it would be great if, in addition to the chain_id parameter, I could also pass the data to the initialization function in R.  The number of parameters in my model depends on the size of the data, and it would be great if I could write a generic initialization function without hard-coding the number of parameters.

Thanks again for the help!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Positive definiteness failure on initialization causes crash rather than rejection
parts:
The other thing you can do is just reassign to
a plain old matrix. But that could fail when passed into
a multivariate probabilty function, which also checks
positive definiteness.

We're going to be rewriting soon after the 2.0 release
to make it much easier to work with the Cholesky factor
basis of either a correlation or covariance matrix. This
is a lot more arithmetically stable.
> also pass the data to the initialization function in R.

Good idea. Today's my day for creating RStan feature requests:

https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/issues/19

R's scope is flexible enough to let your initialization function
depend on the data if it's visible to the function. Or
you could write a program that takes the data as an argument and
returns an init function. I also suggested we might just provide
an instance of how to do the latter and leave the function signature
as is, because I don't know how to do what you suggest while maintaining
backward compatibility.

- Bob
